question: In midwifery, what is the medical term for a normal, uncomplicated vaginal delivery?
explanation: You'll often hear 'eutocia' used to describe a smooth, straightforward birth with no major hitches. It's the exact opposite of dystocia! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: Which of these describes a normal (eutocic) labour?

options.A: Surgical induction with a breech presentation at 35 weeks
options.D: Spontaneous onset with a cephalic presentation at term

explanation: Spot on! For labour to be truly normal, it should start on its own between 37-42 weeks, and the baby's head (cephalic) should come first. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: What is the name for that blood-tinged mucus plug that drops when the cervix starts opening up?
explanation: We call it 'the show'! It's a classic early sign that the cervix is getting ready and opening up for labour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: A mum comes to the clinic having tummy tightening. When she walks around, the contractions stop completely and her cervix is still tightly closed. What's happening?
explanation: These are false labour (or Braxton Hicks) contractions! True labour contractions keep getting stronger even if the mum moves around. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: Why do we perform Leopold's maneuvers when a pregnant woman is admitted?

options.A: To determine the fetal position and presentation
options.B: To measure the mother's blood pressure accurately
options.C: To check if the amniotic fluid is clear or meconium-stained
options.D: To measure the exact cervical dilation in centimeters

explanation: Leopold's maneuvers are just our hands-on way of feeling the mum's tummy to figure out how the baby is lying inside. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: When a mum gets admitted to the labour ward, why is checking her antenatal card so important?

options.A: To determine the exact time the baby will be born
options.B: To find out if the mother attended antenatal classes regularly
options.C: To identify pre-existing risk factors and review past test results
options.D: To calculate the hospital bill for the delivery service

explanation: Her antenatal card holds secrets to a safe delivery! It shows her blood group, scan results, and any risks we need to watch out for. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: At what point does the first stage of labour officially end?
explanation: The first stage is all about opening up. Once the cervix hits 10 cm (fully dilated), stage one wraps up and it's time to push! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: Which stage of labour has the highest risk for heavy bleeding (postpartum hemorrhage)?
explanation: The fourth stage is the immediate hour or two after delivery. We monitor mums extra closely here because the uterus needs to clamp down firmly to stop bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: During birth, the baby's chin tucks tightly against its chest. What is this movement called?
explanation: That tucking action is called flexion! It helps the smallest part of the baby's head lead the way through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: Why does the baby's head need to twist (internal rotation) as it travels down the birth canal?

options.A: To stimulate the onset of maternal pushing reflexes
options.B: To ensure the placenta detaches from the uterine wall
options.C: To adapt to the changing shape and wider dimensions of the pelvic outlet
options.D: To prevent early rupture of the amniotic membranes

explanation: The pelvis changes shape from top to bottom, so the baby has to twist slightly to fit through the widest parts easily. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: What is the name of the special chart midwives use to track how labour is progressing?
explanation: The partograph is our best friend in the labour ward! It gives a clear picture of how labour is moving along so we spot trouble early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: A mum in early labour hasn't peed in over three hours. What should you as the nurse do?

options.A: Encourage her to empty her bladder to prevent delayed fetal descent
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake for the remainder of the labour process
options.C: Perform an emergency vaginal examination to check cervical dilation
options.D: Administer an intravenous diuretic medication immediately

explanation: A full bladder can actually push the baby's head out of position and slow down contractions. Always encourage her to pee! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: Which of these is a natural, drug-free way to help a mum cope with labour pain?
explanation: Massages, warm water (hydrotherapy), and breathing exercises work wonders for natural pain relief without medications. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: What is the big danger of giving strong pain meds (opioids) right before the baby is born?
explanation: If opioids cross the placenta right before birth, they can make it hard for the newborn to take its first good breath. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: At what exact times do we check a newborn's Apgar score?

options.A: At birth and every hour for four hours
options.C: Immediately upon crowning and at delivery

explanation: We check at 1 minute to see how the baby tolerated birth, and again at 5 minutes to see how they're adjusting to the outside world. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)

question: Why do we place a newborn straight onto the mum's bare chest right after birth?

options.A: To promote thermal regulation and early bonding
options.B: To prevent the baby from crying loudly
options.C: To speed up the delivery of the placenta
options.D: To measure the birth weight accurately

explanation: Skin-to-skin contact uses mum's body warmth to keep the baby cozy while helping them bond and start breastfeeding early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)
